opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely exciting direction, but I try to separate the hype from the actual research questions underneath it.

The strongest argument for humanoids is that the world is built for human bodies. Our kitchens, warehouses, door handles, and stairs all assume roughly our shape and reach. If you want one general-purpose machine that can operate across all those environments without rebuilding the environment, the humanoid form factor makes a lot of sense. There's also a data argument: we have an enormous amount of video of humans doing things, and the closer a robot's embodiment is to ours, the easier it may be to transfer from that data, whether through imitation, teleoperation, or learning from observation.

That said, I'm a bit skeptical of the idea that the body is the hard part. In my experience, the bottleneck has mostly been intelligence, not hardware. We've had capable arms and mobile bases for a long time, and we still struggle to get robust, generalizable manipulation in messy, unstructured settings. Putting legs and a torso on the problem doesn't automatically solve that. In some ways it makes things harder: you add balance, more degrees of freedom, more failure modes, higher cost, and more safety concerns, especially around people.

So my view is that humanoids are a reasonable long-term bet, but the near-term value will probably come from whoever cracks the "brain" side: foundation models for robotics, better use of multimodal pretraining, scalable data collection, and evaluation that reflects real-world reliability rather than curated demos. Those advances should transfer across embodiments anyway, which is part of why I think cross-embodiment learning is so important.

I'd also caution people to watch demos critically. A lot of what you see is teleoperated or heavily scripted, which is fine for showing hardware capability, but it's not the same as autonomy. The real milestone is a robot doing useful, varied work for hours in an environment it hasn't seen, with a low intervention rate, at a cost that makes economic sense. We're not there yet, but the amount of capital and talent flowing in is real, and that tends to accelerate things. I'm optimistic, just with a healthy dose of realism about timelines.

r001.rationale: The response calls humanoids an exciting direction and a reasonable long-term bet for general-purpose robotics, but it does not frame the push toward humanoids as a way to make robotics an AGI problem.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest turn now.

Thanks for having me. I think humanoids are an interesting bet, but I'd separate the hype from the actual research question underneath it.

The strongest argument for the form factor is that the world is built for humans. Doorknobs, stairs, kitchen counters, tools, all of it is sized and shaped for our bodies. So if you want one robot that can go into any environment and be useful without redesigning the environment, a humanoid is a reasonable target. There's also a data argument: humans generate an enormous amount of video of humans doing things, and the closer your embodiment is to a human, the easier it is in principle to transfer from that data.

Where I get more skeptical is the assumption that the hardware is the hard part, or that solving the body solves the problem. The bottleneck in robotics right now isn't that we lack a two-legged chassis. It's that we don't have robust, general policies that can perceive a messy scene, understand what's being asked, and act reliably across long horizons. A humanoid form actually makes some of that harder. You're adding balance, more degrees of freedom, higher cost, and more ways to fail, before you've demonstrated the intelligence layer works on simpler platforms.

So my honest assessment is that humanoids are a great forcing function and probably where a lot of the industry ends up, but as a research direction I'd be careful about letting the form factor drive the agenda. The thing worth pushing on is general-purpose robot learning: foundation models that span embodiments, scaling data collection, getting the sim-to-real and real-world evaluation story right. If you solve that, the humanoid becomes one deployment target among many. If you don't, you have a very expensive, very impressive-looking robot that still can't fold laundry in a house it hasn't seen.

The other thing I'd flag is that progress gets measured by demos, and humanoids produce extremely compelling demos. That's not nothing, it attracts talent and capital. But it can also create a gap between what people think is solved and what is actually solved, and the field has been burned by that before.

r001.rationale: The response calls humanoids a reasonable target and a useful forcing function, but frames the key research challenge as general-purpose robot learning across embodiments. It does not present humanoid robotics as a direction for making robotics an AGI problem.

astra-6.text:
I think humanoid robotics is an exciting research direction, but I would separate the question of the robot’s form from the question of its intelligence. A humanoid is appealing because our environments are designed around people. There’s a practical argument for having a robot that can reach the same shelves and use the same tools that we do.

But the form factor alone doesn’t solve the hard problems. You still need a system that can understand a task, manipulate unfamiliar objects, and recover when something goes wrong. And adding legs introduces a lot of complexity if what you’re really trying to study is manipulation or generalization.

So I’m enthusiastic about humanoids, but I don’t think every robotics research effort needs to converge on that embodiment. I’d judge the progress by how reliably the robot can perform useful tasks across different environments, and how much additional training it needs for a new task. That’s more informative to me than whether it looks human or produces an impressive demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response calls humanoid robotics exciting and discusses task understanding and generalization, but it does not frame the push as making robotics an AGI problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think humanoids are a really exciting research direction, but I would separate the question of the robot’s form from the question of its intelligence. A humanoid body gives you a useful starting point because our environments are designed around people. But having that body doesn’t automatically give you the ability to do useful work reliably.

The research question that interests me is how we get robots to generalize: to handle an object they haven’t seen before, recover when something goes wrong, and carry out a task in a new environment. Humanoids can be a great platform for studying that, but so can simpler robots. You can learn a lot about manipulation without also having to solve balance and locomotion.

So I’m optimistic about the push, especially if it brings more investment and better hardware into robotics. I’d just judge progress by what the robot can actually do, how reliably it can do it, and how much human intervention it needs. Those are more meaningful measures than how human it looks.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls humanoids an exciting research direction and discusses robot generalization, but does not connect the push to making robotics an AGI problem.
